lines: One new consumer joins a group, and suddenly nobody in that group is reading anything at all.
Not just the new member catching up — every single consumer, frozen, waiting for the whole group to settle.
That's a design choice, not an inevitability, and this topic is about exactly what that choice costs and how it changed.
A consumer's committed offset isn't some side-channel bookkeeping value — it's a record, written into a log, the same kind of log this chapter keeps coming back to.
That log stays compacted down to just the latest offset per consumer, so constant commits never make it grow without bound.
On top of that log sits a much messier problem: dividing a topic's partitions fairly among a group of consumers that come and go.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Growing a group by one member only ever forces some partitions to change hands, never all of them at once.
Does every member's consumption pause while that happens, or only the members whose own assignment actually changes?
answer: It depends entirely on which protocol the group is running — and that's the whole point of this topic.
Under the older protocol, every member pauses, whether its own partitions moved or not.
Under the newer approach, only the members whose assignment actually changed ever pause at all.

lines: Here's a real reassignment, not a hypothetical one: the same eight-to-nine scale-up, computed for real.
Most of the group keeps exactly the partitions it already had.
Only a small handful of members actually hand anything off to make room for the new one.
Run that same scale-up under two different rules for who gets to keep consuming.
The older rule pauses the entire group, every member, without exception.
The newer rule pauses only the handful that reassignment actually touched — everyone else never even notices.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal settles it.
A consumer restarts briefly, but it's configured with a persistent identity it keeps across restarts.
Does that brief restart still force the whole group to rebalance?
answer: Not if it comes back quickly enough.
A persistent configured identity means the coordinator treats the group's membership as unchanged the whole time it's gone, not just that the rejoin happens to be fast.
Wait too long, past the configured timeout, and it's treated as a real departure — rebalanced like anyone else.

lines: Three restarts, run for real, side by side.
No persistent identity at all: a rebalance, every time, no matter how fast the restart was.
A persistent identity and a fast restart: nothing happens. The same identity after a slow restart: rebalanced anyway.
The newer protocol doesn't just change who gets paused — it moves the actual computation of who owns what onto the broker itself.
Kafka Streams gets that same broker-driven shape through its own dedicated protocol.
That one comes with its own stated rough edges for now, not a complete drop-in replacement yet.
Every number in this reel so far came from one real run of this topic's own toy rebalance model, happening just now.

The paused-member counts under both protocols, and every one of those static-membership restart outcomes.
So: a committed offset is just another record in a log this chapter already knows how to build.
A membership change no longer has to stop everyone — only the members it actually touches.
A persistent identity skips the pause entirely when it isn't needed, and that same broker-driven shape now reaches Kafka Streams too.
